Text.name: guidelines
Text.value: Read the question and answer, then determine if it contains the following features:

View.style: margin-left: 1em; margin-top: 1em; padding: 0.5em; background: #f8f9fa; border-left: 3px solid #6c757d;

Text.name: humor_def
Text.value: HUMOR includes explicit jokes AND ironic language.

Text.name: humor_look_for
Text.value: ✓ Look for:

Text.name: humor_1
Text.value: • Explicit jokes (with or without a punchline)

Text.name: humor_2
Text.value: • Puns or wordplay meant to amuse

Text.name: humor_3
Text.value: • Ironic language: understatement, tongue-in-cheek, wry observations

Text.name: humor_ex_header
Text.value: ✓ Examples of humor PRESENT:

Text.name: humor_ex1
Text.value: • '...killing our own cells, which wouldn't be very wise' (ironic understatement)

Text.name: humor_ex2
Text.value: • 'Atoms are like tiny LEGO blocks, except you can't step on them at 3 AM' (joke)

Text.name: humor_ex3
Text.value: • 'Why did the electron leave the atom? Because it had no potential' (pun)

Text.name: humor_ex4
Text.value: • 'Evolution doesn't plan ahead – if it did, it would have given us better knees' (ironic)

Text.name: humor_not_header
Text.value: ✗ NOT humor:

Text.name: humor_not1
Text.value: • Creative analogies/metaphors without irony

Text.name: humor_not2
Text.value: • Engaging tone without actual jokes

Text.name: humor_not3
Text.value: • Personification without irony

Text.name: humor_not4
Text.value: • Playful language lacking actual jokes or ironic statements

View.style: margin-left: 1em; margin-top: 1em; padding: 0.5em; background: #f8f9fa; border-left: 3px solid #6c757d;

Text.name: analogy_def
Text.value: An ANALOGY explicitly compares TWO DIFFERENT DOMAINS to explain a concept.

Text.name: analogy_must_have
Text.value: ✓ Must have all three:

Text.name: analogy_1
Text.value: • SOURCE: a familiar, concrete situation (e.g., 'a library', 'traffic on a highway')

Text.name: analogy_2
Text.value: • TARGET: the scientific/abstract concept being explained

Text.name: analogy_3
Text.value: • EXPLICIT comparison words: 'like', 'similar to', 'just as', 'think of X as Y', 'imagine', 'consider'

Text.name: analogy_ex_header
Text.value: ✓ Examples of analogies:

Text.name: analogy_ex1
Text.value: • 'Think of DNA like a recipe book' (source: recipe book → target: DNA)

Text.name: analogy_ex2
Text.value: • 'The immune system works like an army defending a castle'

Text.name: analogy_ex3
Text.value: • 'Electrons orbit the nucleus similar to how planets orbit the sun'

Text.name: analogy_not_header
Text.value: ✗ NOT analogies:

Text.name: analogy_not1
Text.value: • Simple examples without cross-domain comparison

Text.name: analogy_not2
Text.value: • Within-domain comparisons ('Viruses are smaller than bacteria')

Text.name: analogy_not3
Text.value: • Metaphors without explicit comparison markers ('The brain is a computer')

View.style: margin-left: 1em; margin-top: 1em; padding: 0.5em; background: #f8f9fa; border-left: 3px solid #6c757d;

Text.name: metaphor_def
Text.value: A METAPHOR describes one thing AS IF it were another, WITHOUT explicit comparison words. Metaphors use figurative language that would be literally false but conveys meaning through imagery.

Text.name: metaphor_clear_header
Text.value: ✓ CLEAR METAPHORS:

Text.name: metaphor_type1
Text.value: • Direct identity statements: 'The cell is a factory', 'Genes are blueprints', 'The brain is a computer'

Text.name: metaphor_type2
Text.value: • Strong personification with IMPOSSIBLE actions: 'The virus wants to spread', 'Evolution designed this', 'Nature selected for traits'

Text.name: metaphor_type2_note
Text.value: (These attribute intention/desire to entities that cannot literally have them)

Text.name: metaphor_type3
Text.value: • Cross-domain vocabulary used figuratively: 'genetic code contains instructions', 'cellular machinery', 'molecular scissors'

Text.name: metaphor_ex_header
Text.value: ✓ Examples of metaphors:

Text.name: metaphor_ex1
Text.value: • 'The heart is a pump' → METAPHOR (heart literally called a pump)

Text.name: metaphor_ex2
Text.value: • 'Cancer cells are invaders' → METAPHOR (cells assigned military role)

Text.name: metaphor_ex3
Text.value: • 'Beyond that lie dragons' → METAPHOR (figurative danger/unknown)

Text.name: metaphor_ex4
Text.value: • 'Zombie-proteins that reanimate' → METAPHOR (proteins described as zombies)

Text.name: metaphor_not_header
Text.value: ✗ NOT metaphors (exclude all of these):

Text.name: metaphor_not1
Text.value: • SIMILES/ANALOGIES: comparisons with 'like', 'similar to', 'imagine', 'think of it as'

Text.name: metaphor_not2
Text.value: • IDIOMS: frozen phrases with conventional figurative meanings that native speakers would recognize as common sayings (e.g., 'play mind tricks', 'tip of the iceberg', 'here be dragons')

Text.name: metaphor_not3
Text.value: • METONYMY: organizations standing for their people ('The USA wants' = government wants, 'The company decided')

Text.name: metaphor_not4
Text.value: • WEAK PERSONIFICATION: animals, systems, or abstractions with common traits ('cats figured out', 'server checks', 'the market fears')

Text.name: metaphor_not5
Text.value: • SHAPE DESCRIPTIONS: literal visual resemblance ('potato-shaped asteroid', 'mushroom cloud')

Text.name: metaphor_not6
Text.value: • TECHNICAL TERMS & DEAD METAPHORS: standardized vocabulary, including terms used literally in their original domain ('shock wave', 'chain reaction' in physics) or so conventionalized they no longer feel figurative ('genetic code', 'viral marketing')

Text.name: metaphor_not7
Text.value: • LITERAL STATEMENTS: 'The heart pumps blood', 'Fields attract and repel'

Text.name: metaphor_key_rule_header
Text.value: ⚠️ KEY DECISION RULE:

Text.name: metaphor_key_rule
Text.value: Ask: 'Is this phrase NOVEL to this context, or would a native speaker recognize it as a common expression?'

Text.name: metaphor_key_rule1
Text.value: • If a native speaker would say 'oh, that's a common saying' → NOT a metaphor (it's an idiom)

Text.name: metaphor_key_rule2
Text.value: • If the figurative language is FRESH and INVENTED for this explanation → METAPHOR

Text.name: metaphor_key_rule3
Text.value: Only count ACTIVE metaphors that create fresh figurative meaning.

Text.name: metaphor_key_rule4
Text.value: Exclude idioms, explicit analogies, weak personification, or technical terms.

View.style: margin-left: 1em; margin-top: 1em; padding: 0.5em; background: #f8f9fa; border-left: 3px solid #6c757d;

Text.name: connection_def
Text.value: An EXPLICIT reference to a NAMED external entity.

Text.name: connection_look_for
Text.value: ✓ Look for named references to:

Text.name: connection_1
Text.value: • Specific news/current events: 'the H1N1 outbreak', 'the 2008 financial crisis'

Text.name: connection_2
Text.value: • Named historical events: 'World War II', 'the Chernobyl disaster'

Text.name: connection_3
Text.value: • Public figures, brands, culture: 'Einstein', 'Tesla', 'Star Wars'

Text.name: connection_not_header
Text.value: ✗ NOT connections:

Text.name: connection_not1
Text.value: • Generic examples without named entities ('like boiling water')

Text.name: connection_not2
Text.value: • Vague references ('as we all know', 'in everyday life')

Text.name: connection_not3
Text.value: • Scientific analogies or metaphors

Text.name: connection_not4
Text.value: • References already in the original question

View.style: margin-left: 1em; margin-top: 1em; padding: 0.5em; background: #f8f9fa; border-left: 3px solid #6c757d;

Text.name: scaffolding_def
Text.value: The explanation builds understanding INCREMENTALLY in a logical sequence.

Text.name: scaffolding_look_for
Text.value: ✓ Look for:

Text.name: scaffolding_1
Text.value: • A clear starting point (basic concept or motivation)

Text.name: scaffolding_2
Text.value: • Progressive steps that build on each other

Text.name: scaffolding_3
Text.value: • Each step is appropriately sized (not too big a jump)

Text.name: scaffolding_4
Text.value: • Reader can follow logical development from simple → complex

Text.name: scaffolding_ex_present_header
Text.value: ✓ Example PRESENT:

Text.name: scaffolding_ex_present
Text.value: 'Two facts motivate my research—first, diverse systems are healthier... My research asks if it matters that species are being gained and lost... By manipulating plant number and type, I can uncover the mechanisms...'

Text.name: scaffolding_ex_present_why
Text.value: → motivation → question → method (clear progression)

Text.name: scaffolding_ex_absent_header
Text.value: ✗ Example ABSENT:

Text.name: scaffolding_ex_absent
Text.value: 'My research uses plant manipulation experiments to study biodiversity mechanisms in communities where species turnover affects ecosystem health.'

Text.name: scaffolding_ex_absent_why
Text.value: → All concepts at once, no progressive building
